O coração e o fígado de Mercy foram queimados, e as cinzas, misturadas com água, viraram um tônico para Edwin. Ele morreu dois meses depois. Alguns estudiosos especulam, sem prova direta, que Bram Stoker soube do caso pelos jornais e se inspirou nele para criar a personagem Lucy Westenra, de "Drácula". E, provavelmente, as famílias nem chamavam os mortos de vampiros: o termo era dos jornais e de gente de fora.

fontes.trecho: The Mercy Brown vampire incident occurred in Rhode Island in January 1892. It is one of the best documented cases of the exhumation of a corpse in order to perform rituals to banish an undead manifestation. [...] Mary Eliza was the first to die of the disease on December 8, 1883, followed on June 6, 1884, by her eldest daughter Mary Olive at age 20, according to her grave stone. In 1891, daughter Mercy Lena Brown and only son Edwin "Eddie" Atwood Brown also contracted the disease. [...] As superstition dictated, Mercy's heart and liver were burned, and the ashes were mixed with water to create a tonic which was given to Edwin in an effort to resolve his illness and stop the influence of the undead. The young man died two months later. [...] Scholars have suggested that Bram Stoker knew about the Mercy Brown case through newspaper articles and based the character Lucy Westenra upon her in his novel Dracula.

The New England vampire panic was the reaction to an outbreak of tuberculosis in the late 18th and 19th centuries throughout Rhode Island, eastern Connecticut, southern Massachusetts, Vermont, and other areas of the New England states. [...] Tuberculosis was known as "consumption" at the time, as it appeared to consume an infected person's body. It is now known to be a bacterial disease, but the cause was unknown until the late 19th century. The infection spreads easily among a family; thus, when one family member died of consumption, other members were often infected and gradually lost their health. People believed that this was due to the deceased TB sufferer draining the life from other family members. [...] The corpse was deemed to be feeding on the living if it was determined to be unusually fresh, especially if the heart or other organs contained liquid blood. [...] Two months after Mercy's death, her father George Brown—who did not believe that a vampire was to blame—reluctantly permitted others to exhume the bodies of his family. [...] It is unlikely that the deceased would have been known as vampires by their affected families, because the word was not in common use in the community at that time. However, the term was used by newspapers and outsiders at the time

gancho: Segundo a lenda, o trono de coroação dos reis dinamarqueses é de chifre de unicórnio. É de presas de narval: por séculos, esse dente comprido de um mamífero marinho foi vendido na Europa como chifre do bicho mítico.
explicacao: O trono foi feito entre 1662 e 1671, logo depois que a Dinamarca e a Noruega adotaram a monarquia absoluta, e serviu nas coroações de 1671 a 1840. Fica no Castelo de Rosenborg, em Copenhague, guardado por três leões de prata em tamanho natural. O material era tido como um dos bens mais valiosos que alguém podia ter: "chifres de unicórnio" eram dados como presentes diplomáticos, e lascas e pó deles eram vendidos em boticas como antídoto universal até o século XVIII. Segundo o cirurgião francês Ambroise Paré, na corte do rei da França eles serviam para detectar veneno na comida e na bebida. A fonte real era o narval, um mamífero marinho cuja "presa" é, na verdade, um dente alongado, presente nos machos e em algumas fêmeas. Vikings e nórdicos da Groenlândia provavelmente começaram esse comércio. Até a Bíblia entrou na história: o re'em, animal citado nove vezes na Bíblia hebraica, virou "unicórnio" na Vulgata latina, e a Bíblia inglesa do rei Jaime seguiu essa tradução no livro de Jó. Alguns estudiosos defendem que o re'em era, na verdade, o auroque, um boi selvagem.

fontes.trecho: According to legend, the Coronation Chair is made of the horn of unicorns. In reality, it is made from Norwegian narwhal tusks. It is guarded by three life-size silver lions [...] The Coronation Chair is located in the Castle of Rosenborg in Copenhagen. [...] Following the 1660 introduction of absolute monarchy in Denmark and Norway, King Frederick III (r. 1648–1670) ordered a coronation chair to be created. The Coronation Chair was made between 1662 and 1671 by Bendix Grodtschilling. [...] The Coronation Chair was used at coronations between 1671, for Christian V, and 1840.

Seen as one of the most valuable assets that a person could possess, unicorn horns were given as diplomatic gifts, and chips and dust from them could be purchased at apothecaries as universal antidotes until the 18th century. [...] This marine mammal is the true bearer of the alicorn, actually an extended tooth found in the mouth of males and some females. [...] Ambroise Paré explains that alicorns were used in the court of the King of France to detect the presence of poison in food and drink
Vikings and Greenland Norse likely began the trade of narwhal tusks

is an animal mentioned nine times in the Hebrew Bible. It has been translated as "unicorn" in the Latin Vulgate, King James Version [...] Natan Slifkin has argued that the re'em was an aurochs, as has Isaac Asimov before him. [...] The King James Version of the Book of Job followed the Septuagint and Jerome's Vulgate in the translation of re'em into unicorn [...] interpret re'em as "wild ox" or "wild bull".

gancho: O chupacabra surgiu em Porto Rico em 1995. Segundo um investigador, a testemunha que deu a descrição original tinha visto antes o filme de terror "Species", cujo monstro é quase idêntico ao relato dela.
explicacao: Em março de 1995, oito ovelhas foram achadas mortas em Porto Rico, cada uma com três perfurações no peito e, segundo se dizia, sem nenhum sangue. Em agosto, uma moradora de Canóvanas, Madelyne Tolentino, relatou ter visto a criatura, em meio a uma onda de mortes de animais; só naquele ano, os relatos na ilha passaram de 200. O nome, "chupa-cabras", é atribuído ao humorista porto-riquenho Silverio Pérez, que o cunhou num programa de rádio. O investigador Benjamin Radford passou cinco anos no caso e concluiu, num livro de 2011, que a descrição de Tolentino se baseava em Sil, a criatura alienígena do filme "Species", de 1995. Ela tinha visto o filme antes do relato e disse que a semelhança era impressionante. Segundo Radford, ela acreditava que o que aparecia no filme estava acontecendo de verdade em Porto Rico, e por isso a descrição mais importante do chupacabra não merece confiança. Nenhuma necropsia confirmou que os animais tinham sido drenados: um veterinário do Departamento de Agricultura porto-riquenho analisou 300 supostas vítimas e viu que elas não estavam sem sangue. Nos EUA, os "chupacabras" examinados costumam ser coiotes e cães com sarna grave.

fontes.trecho: The first reported attack later associated with the chupacabras phenomenon occurred in Puerto Rico in March 1995. Eight sheep were found dead, each reportedly bearing three puncture wounds to the chest and alleged to have been completely drained of blood. Several months later, in August, a resident named Madelyne Tolentino reported a sighting of the creature in the municipality of Canóvanas. [...] The first reports from Puerto Rico numbered more than 200 in 1995. [...] The name is generally attributed to Puerto Rican comedian Silverio Pérez, who coined the term in 1995 while discussing the reported livestock attacks during his radio program in San Juan. [...] A five-year investigation by Benjamin Radford, documented in his 2011 book Tracking the Chupacabra, concluded that the description given by the original eyewitness in Puerto Rico, Madelyne Tolentino, was based on the creature Sil in the 1995 science-fiction horror film Species. The alien creature Sil is nearly identical to Tolentino's chupacabra eyewitness account and she had seen the movie before her report: "It was a creature that looked like the chupacabra, with spines on its back and all... The resemblance to the chupacabra was really impressive", Tolentino reported. Radford revealed that Tolentino "believed that the creatures and events she saw in Species were happening in reality in Puerto Rico at the time", and therefore concludes that "the most important chupacabra description cannot be trusted". [...] The reports of blood-sucking by the chupacabra were never confirmed by a necropsy, the only way to conclude that the animal was drained of blood. Dr. David Morales, a Puerto Rican veterinarian with the Department of Agriculture, analyzed 300 reported victims of the chupacabra and found that they had not been bled dry. [...] Investigations of purported sightings in northern Mexico and the Southern United States have instead identified the animals involved as canids afflicted by severe mange.

gancho: O Slender Man, figura de terror alta e sem rosto, tem data de nascimento: 10 de junho de 2009, num concurso de montagens "paranormais" num fórum da internet. Folcloristas o estudam como um mito que se viu nascer.
explicacao: O autor foi Eric Knudsen, sob o pseudônimo Victor Surge. Ele pegou duas fotos em preto e branco de grupos de crianças e acrescentou uma figura alta e magra, de terno preto. Os participantes anteriores tinham postado só fotos; ele juntou trechos de supostos testemunhos sobre o sumiço de crianças e deu à criatura o nome de "Slender Man". A partir daí, outros usuários foram ampliando a história. Um dos primeiros acréscimos foi um conto passado na Alemanha do século XVI, com um personagem chamado Der Großman, apresentado como se fosse um registro antigo da mesma figura. Sem cânone oficial, o personagem se espalhou por séries de vídeo, jogos e filmes, e inspirou o Enderman do Minecraft. Para vários estudiosos, ele é uma forma de folclore digital, mesmo sendo ficção com origem identificável: foi criado de forma coletiva, muda conforme quem conta e se molda à reação do público. A pesquisadora Shira Chess observa que, ao contrário de vampiros e lobisomens, a formação desse mito pode ser rastreada, o que ajuda a entender como mitos e folclore se formam. Já o folclorista Jeff Tolbert vê aí o caminho inverso do habitual: em vez de encenar uma lenda que já existia, criou-se um conjunto de narrativas com cara de tradição onde não havia nenhuma.

fontes.trecho: The Slender Man also inspired the Enderman in Minecraft. [...] The Slender Man was created on 10 June 2009, on a thread in the Something Awful Internet forum. The thread was a Photoshop contest in which users were challenged to create "paranormal images". Forum poster Eric Knudsen, under the pseudonym "Victor Surge", contributed two black-and-white images of groups of children to which he added a tall, thin, spectral figure wearing a black suit. Although previous entries had consisted solely of photographs, Surge supplemented his submission with snatches of text—supposedly from witnesses—describing the abductions of groups of children and giving the character the name "the Slender Man" [...] Subsequent posters expanded upon the character, adding their own visual or textual contributions. [...] One of the earliest additions was added by a forum user named "Thoreau-Up", who created a folklore story set in 16th-century Germany involving a character called Der Großman, which was implied by the writer to be an early reference to the Slender Man. [...] Several scholars have argued that, despite being a fictional work with an identifiable origin point, the Slender Man represents a form of digital folklore. Shira Chess argues that Slender Man exemplifies the similarities between traditional folklore and the open source ethos of the Internet, and that, unlike those of traditional monsters such as vampires and werewolves, the fact that the Slender Man's mythos can be tracked and signposted offers a powerful insight into how myth and folklore form. Chess identifies three aspects of the Slender Man mythos that tie it to folklore: collectivity (meaning that it is created by a collective, rather than a single individual), variability (meaning that the story changes depending on the teller), and performance (meaning that the storyteller's narrative changes to reflect the audience's response). [...] Jeff Tolbert also accepts the Slender Man as folkloric, and suggests it represents a process he calls "reverse ostension". Ostension in folkloristics is the process of acting out a folk narrative. According to Tolbert, the Slender Man does the opposite by creating a set of folklore-like narratives where none existed before.

gancho: Por cerca de mil anos, cristãos veneraram um santo que era, na prática, o Buda. A vida de São Josafá é uma versão cristianizada da história de Sidarta Gautama, e o nome Josafá vem de "bodisatva".
explicacao: Na lenda, um rei da Índia que perseguia cristãos ouve de astrólogos que o filho, o príncipe Josafá, um dia se converteria. Ele isola o rapaz, mas o eremita Barlaam o encontra e o converte. No fim, o próprio rei se converte, e o príncipe abdica para viver em retiro com o velho mestre. A história fez uma longa viagem. Partiu de um texto budista em sânscrito dos séculos II a IV, passou por uma versão maniqueísta e por um livro árabe que circulava em Bagdá no século VIII, e foi cristianizada num épico georgiano do século X. Um monge georgiano a traduziu para o grego antes de 1028, e em 1048 ela ganhou versão latina. O nome mudou pelo caminho: o sânscrito "bodisatva" virou Bodisav em textos do persa médio e Budhasaf em árabe, onde um ponto duplicado na escrita trocou o "b" por "y". Depois veio Iodasaph, em georgiano, Ioasaph, em grego, e enfim Josaphat, em latim. Barlaam e Josafá entraram no calendário ortodoxo e em edições antigas do Martirológio Romano. Houve quem notasse a semelhança antes, como um manuscrito de Marco Polo e o cronista português Diogo do Couto, mas só em 1859-1860 pesquisadores europeus estabeleceram que, em Josafá, o Buda vinha sendo venerado como santo cristão havia cerca de mil anos. Uma cena da lenda, a das três caixinhas, chegou até "O Mercador de Veneza", de Shakespeare.

fontes.trecho: According to tradition, an Indian king persecuted the Christian Church in his realm. After astrologers predicted that his own son would some day become a Christian, the king imprisoned the young prince Josaphat, who nevertheless met the hermit Saint Barlaam and converted to Christianity. After much tribulation the young prince's father accepted the Christian faith, turned over his throne to Josaphat, and retired to the desert to become a hermit. Josaphat himself later abdicated and went into seclusion with his old teacher Barlaam. The story is thought to be a Christianized and later version of the story of Siddhartha Gautama, who became the Buddha. [...] The tale derives from a second to fourth century Sanskrit Mahayana Buddhist text, via a Manichaean version, then the Arabic Kitāb Bilawhar wa-Būd̠āsaf (Book of Bilawhar and Budhasaf), current in Baghdad in the eighth century, from where it entered into Middle Eastern Christian circles before appearing in European versions. The first Christianized adaptation was the Georgian epic Balavariani dating back to the 10th century. A Georgian monk, Euthymius of Athos, translated the story into Greek, some time before he died in an accident while visiting Constantinople in 1028. There the Greek adaptation was translated into Latin in 1048 [...] a scene there involving three caskets eventually appeared, via Caxton's English translation of a Latin version, in Shakespeare's "The Merchant of Venice". [...] In this context, the name Josaphat is derived from the Sanskrit bodhisattva. The Sanskrit word was changed to Bodisav in Middle Persian texts in the 6th or 7th century, then to Būdhasaf or Yūdhasaf in an 8th-century Arabic document (Arabic initial "b" ﺑ changed to "y" ﻳ by duplication of a dot in handwriting). This became Iodasaph in Georgian in the 10th century, and that name was adapted as Ioasaph (Ἰωάσαφ) in Greece in the 11th century, and then was assimilated to Iosaphat/Josaphat in Latin. [...] Barlaam and Josaphat were included in earlier editions of the Roman Martyrology [...] Barlaam and Josaphat were entered into the Greek Orthodox liturgical calendar [...] "But not till the mid-nineteenth century was it recognised that, in Josaphat, the Buddha had been venerated as a Christian saint for about a thousand years." This was ascertained through the researches of Edouard de Laboulaye and Felix Liebrecht in 1859-1860. [...] One of the Marco Polo manuscripts notes the remarkable similarity between the tale of "Sergamoni Borcan" (i.e. Sakyamuni Burkhan; the name that Polo recorded the Mongols using for the Buddha) and St. Josaphat [...] e a identificação, por Diogo do Couto (1542–1616), de Josaphate com o Buda.

gancho: Uma Cinderela chinesa escrita por volta de 850 já tinha madrasta cruel, sapatinho perdido e um rei à procura da dona. Antes ainda, o grego Estrabão registrou uma história de sandália que leva uma moça a casar com o rei.
explicacao: A versão chinesa é a de Ye Xian, publicada numa coletânea da dinastia Tang compilada por Duan Chengshi. Órfã, a moça vira serva da madrasta e da meia-irmã e tem como amigo um peixe, espírito protetor enviado pela mãe morta. A madrasta mata o peixe, mas os ossos dele realizam os desejos de Ye Xian: um vestido de seda verde-mar, um manto de penas de martim-pescador e sapatinhos de ouro. Ela perde um deles numa festa, e o sapato chega às mãos de um rei, fascinado pelo tamanho minúsculo, que manda procurar a moça em cujo pé ele caiba. A versão grega, a de Ródope, costuma ser considerada a mais antiga conhecida: segundo Estrabão, enquanto ela se banhava, uma águia roubou uma de suas sandálias e a largou no colo do rei do Egito, em Mênfis. Intrigado, ele mandou procurar a dona e se casou com ela. Já o sapatinho de vidro é de Perrault. Circula a ideia de que seria um erro: o original seria de "vair", pele de esquilo, confundida com "verre", vidro, algo que Balzac defendeu em 1841. Mas a maioria dos estudiosos acha que o vidro foi uma invenção poética deliberada de Perrault.

fontes.trecho: It is one of the oldest known variants of Cinderella, first published in the Tang dynasty compilation Miscellaneous Morsels from Youyang written around 850 by Duan Chengshi. [...] With her family reduced to poverty, Ye Xian is forced to become a lowly servant and work for her unloving and cruel stepmother, Jin, and spoiled and lazy younger half-sister Jun-Li. [...] The fish was really a guardian spirit sent to her by her own mother, who never forgot her daughter even beyond the grave. [...] She makes a silent wish to the bones, and Ye Xian finds herself clothed magnificently in a gown of sea-green silk, a cloak of kingfisher feathers, and a pair of tiny golden slippers. [...] Fascinated by the shoe's small size, he issues a search to find the maiden whose foot will fit into the shoe and proclaims he will marry that girl.

The earliest known version of the Cinderella story is usually considered to be the Greek story of Rhodopis, as described by the scholar Strabo sometime between 7 BC and 23 AD, about a Greek slave girl who marries the king of Egypt. [...] when [Rhodopis] was bathing, an eagle snatched one of her sandals from her maid and carried it to Memphis; and while the king was administering justice in the open air, the eagle, when it arrived above his head, flung the sandal into his lap; and the king, stirred both by the beautiful shape of the sandal and by the strangeness of the occurrence, sent men in all directions into the country in quest of the woman who wore the sandal; and when she was found in the city of Naucratis, she was brought up to Memphis, and became the wife of the king. [...] Some interpreters, perhaps troubled by sartorial impracticalities, have suggested that Perrault's "glass slipper" (pantoufle de verre) had been a "squirrel fur slipper" (pantoufle de vair) in some unidentified earlier version of the tale, and that Perrault or one of his sources confused the words. However, most scholars believe the glass slipper was a deliberate piece of poetic invention on Perrault's part. [...] Honoré de Balzac wrote in his 1841 philosophical study titled ′Catherine de' Medici′ that Perreault's Cinderella slipper was no doubt of vair

gancho: A Atlântida não foi um continente perdido: foi uma ilha inventada por Platão numa alegoria sobre a arrogância das nações. A ideia de uma supercivilização real perdida deve muito a um autor amador, num livro de 1882.
explicacao: As únicas fontes primárias sobre a Atlântida são dois diálogos de Platão, o Timeu e o Crítias; todas as outras menções vêm deles. Na história, uma potência naval do oeste conquista boa parte da Europa e da Líbia, perde o favor dos deuses depois de uma campanha fracassada contra uma Atenas ficcional e afunda no oceano. Platão criou de propósito um contraste com o Império Aquemênida, a grande potência terrestre do leste, e retratou a Atenas vitoriosa à imagem do Estado ideal da sua "República". O próprio Aristóteles, aluno dele, achava que o mestre tinha inventado a ilha para ensinar filosofia. Hoje, filólogos e estudiosos clássicos concordam que a história é ficção, embora ainda se discuta o que a inspirou. Já na Antiguidade houve quem a tomasse por real, como Estrabão e Posidônio, e a partir do século XVI muitos a ligaram à América. Mas a versão popular de hoje vem do século XIX, quando estudiosos amadores leram Platão como relato histórico. O mais famoso foi Ignatius Donnelly, cujo livro "Atlantis: The Antediluvian World", de 1882, sustentava que todas as civilizações antigas conhecidas descendiam de uma Atlântida tecnologicamente avançada, destruída pelo dilúvio bíblico. Donnelly é apontado como o motivo de o mito durar até hoje. Pouco depois, a fundadora da teosofia, Helena Blavatsky, retomou as ideias dele e afirmou que seu livro de 1888 tinha sido ditado originalmente na Atlântida.

fontes.trecho: is a fictional island mentioned in Plato's works Timaeus and Critias as part of an allegory on the hubris of nations. By describing Atlantis as a naval empire from the west that had conquered most of Europe and Libya, Plato purposely created a literary contrast with the Achaemenid Empire, the great land-based power that ruled the east (what the Greeks called Asia). In Plato's account, Atlantis loses divine favor after an ill-fated campaign against a fictionalized Athens, and subsequently submerges into the Atlantic Ocean. By portraying the victorious Athens in the image of his ideal state from the Republic, Plato intended the Atlantis story to bear witness to the superiority of his concept of a state. [...] nineteenth-century amateur scholars misinterpreted Plato's narrative as historical tradition, most famously Ignatius L. Donnelly in his Atlantis: The Antediluvian World. [...] While present-day philologists and classicists agree on the story's fictional nature, there is still debate on what served as its inspiration. [...] The only primary sources for Atlantis are Plato's dialogues Timaeus and Critias; all other mentions of the island are based on them. [...] Aristotle believed that Plato, his teacher, had invented the island to teach philosophy. [...] The 1882 publication of Atlantis: The Antediluvian World by Ignatius L. Donnelly stimulated much popular interest in Atlantis. He was greatly inspired by early works in Mayanism, and like them, attempted to establish that all known ancient civilizations were descended from Atlantis, which he saw as a technologically sophisticated, more advanced culture. [...] As implied by the title of his book, he also believed that Atlantis was destroyed by the Great Flood mentioned in the Bible. Donnelly is credited as the "father of the nineteenth century Atlantis revival" and is the reason the myth endures today. [...] Helena Petrovna Blavatsky, the founder of the Theosophists, took up Donnelly's interpretations when she wrote The Secret Doctrine (1888), which she claimed was originally dictated in Atlantis. [...] Other ancient historians and philosophers who believed in the existence of Atlantis were Strabo and Posidonius. [...] modern interpretations regarding Atlantis are an amalgamation of diverse, speculative movements that began in the sixteenth century, when scholars began to identify Atlantis with the New World.

gancho: O tântalo, metal de capacitores de computadores, homenageia o Tântalo do mito, que nunca conseguia beber: o metal não absorve ácido. E o nióbio vem de Níobe, filha dele, porque os dois metais são quase gêmeos.
explicacao: O sueco Anders Ekeberg descobriu o tântalo em 1802. No mito grego, Tântalo foi castigado depois da morte a ficar com água pelos joelhos e frutas perfeitas sobre a cabeça: quando se abaixava para beber, a água baixava, e quando estendia a mão, os galhos fugiam. Ekeberg explicou que escolheu o nome em parte pela incapacidade do metal, mergulhado em ácido, de absorver qualquer quantidade dele. A família mítica seguiu na química. Em 1801, o inglês Charles Hatchett tinha achado um elemento parecido e o chamado de colúmbio. Em 1809, William Wollaston concluiu, errado, que os dois eram o mesmo. Em 1846, o alemão Heinrich Rose afirmou haver dois elementos novos no minério de tântalo e os batizou com nomes de filhos de Tântalo: nióbio, de Níobe, e pelópio, de Pélops. O pelópio era só uma mistura, e o nióbio se revelou o mesmo colúmbio de Hatchett. Os dois nomes conviveram por cerca de um século, até que, em 1949, nióbio foi o nome escolhido oficialmente. O nome reflete a enorme semelhança física e química entre os dois elementos, que os torna difíceis de distinguir. Hoje o Brasil é o maior produtor mundial de nióbio.

fontes.trecho: It is named after Tantalus, a figure in Greek mythology. [...] It is used in tantalum capacitors for electronic equipment such as computers. [...] Tantalum was discovered in Sweden in 1802 by Anders Ekeberg [...] In the story, he had been punished after death by being condemned to stand knee-deep in water with perfect fruit growing above his head, both of which eternally tantalized him. (If he bent to drink the water, it drained below the level he could reach, and if he reached for the fruit, the branches moved out of his grasp.) Anders Ekeberg wrote "This metal I call tantalum ... partly in allusion to its incapacity, when immersed in acid, to absorb any and be saturated."

Its name comes from Greek mythology: Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, the namesake of tantalum. The name reflects the great similarity between the two elements in their physical and chemical properties, which makes them difficult to distinguish. English chemist Charles Hatchett reported a new element similar to tantalum in 1801 and named it columbium. In 1809, English chemist William Hyde Wollaston wrongly concluded that tantalum and columbium were identical. [...] for a century both names were used interchangeably. Niobium was officially adopted as the name of the element in 1949 [...] Brazil is the leading producer of niobium and ferroniobium [...] This conclusion was disputed in 1846 by German chemist Heinrich Rose, who argued that there were two different elements in the tantalite sample, and named them after children of Tantalus: niobium (from Niobe) and pelopium (from Pelops). [...] The claimed new elements pelopium, ilmenium, and dianium were in fact identical to niobium or mixtures of niobium and tantalum.

gancho: Um mito dos Klamath, nos EUA, narra a luta de dois deuses que destruiu uma montanha e criou um lago. O lago nasceu mesmo do colapso de um vulcão, há uns 7.700 anos, e já havia gente vivendo ali.
explicacao: O lago é o Crater Lake, no Oregon. Ele ocupa a caldeira formada há cerca de 7.700 anos, quando o vulcão Mount Mazama desabou. A tradição oral dos Klamath fala de uma batalha entre Skell, deus do céu, e Llao, deus do mundo subterrâneo, na qual o Mazama foi destruído, dando origem ao lago, que eles chamam de Giiwas. Segundo essa tradição, os antepassados do povo viram o colapso acontecer. E a arqueologia mostra que a presença humana ali é anterior à erupção: sandálias e outros objetos foram achados sob camadas de cinza e pedra-pomes mais antigas que ela. Na Austrália há um caso possivelmente bem mais antigo. A história da criação do povo Gunditjmara se baseia na erupção do vulcão Budj Bim, quando teria se revelado um ser criador ancestral de mesmo nome. Uma datação publicada em 2020 situou essa erupção em torno de 36.900 anos atrás. Como há artefatos humanos sob as cinzas de outro vulcão da região, de idade parecida, isso também pode ser lido como evidência de que as histórias orais dos Gunditjmara sobre erupções estão entre as tradições orais mais antigas que existem. O Crater Lake segue sagrado para os Klamath.

fontes.trecho: The lake partly fills a 2,148-foot-deep (655 m) caldera that was formed around 7,700 (± 150) years ago by the collapse of the volcano Mount Mazama. [...] A Native American connection with this area has been traced back to before the eruption of Mount Mazama. Archaeologists have found sandals and other artifacts buried under layers of ash, dust, and pumice that antedate the eruption roughly 7,700 years ago. Crater Lake remains significant to the Klamath tribes today. The Klamath name for the lake is Giiwas. [...] The Klamath tribe of Native Americans, whose oral history describes their ancestors witnessing the collapse of Mount Mazama and the formation of Crater Lake, regard the lake as an "abode to the Great Spirit". Klamath oral history tells of a battle between the sky god Skell and the god of the underworld Llao (a prominent feature at Crater Lake is Llao Rock). Mount Mazama was destroyed in the battle, creating Crater Lake, called giiwas in the Klamath language. [...] The tribe still holds Crater Lake in high regard as a spiritual site.

Research published in February 2020 using argon–argon dating, a method of radiometric dating, has dated the eruption at around 36,900 years ago. Specifically, Budj Bim was dated at within 3,100 years either side of 36,900 years BP, and Tower Hill was dated at within 3,800 years either side of 36,800 years BP. Significantly, owing to the presence of human artefacts found under volcanic ash at Tower Hill, this is a "minimum age constraint for human presence in Victoria", and also could be interpreted as evidence for the Gunditjmara oral histories which tell of volcanic eruptions being some of the oldest oral traditions in existence. [...] The creation story of the local Gunditjmara people is based on the eruption of the volcano more than 30,000 years ago. It was via this event that an ancestral creator-being known as Budj Bim was revealed.

gancho: Na lenda do flautista de Hamelin, os ratos só entraram por volta de 1559. Os relatos mais antigos falam apenas de 130 crianças que sumiram da cidade em 1284, e até hoje não se sabe o que aconteceu com elas.
explicacao: A menção mais antiga parece ser um vitral posto na igreja de Hamelin, na Alemanha, por volta de 1300. Ele foi descrito em vários relatos até ser destruído, em 1660, e mostrava uma figura de roupa colorida e crianças vestidas de branco. Em geral, é visto como memória de uma tragédia real da cidade. Um manuscrito de meados do século XV, achado em 1936 nos arquivos de Lüneburg, conta que, no dia dos santos João e Paulo de 1284, um rapaz de uns 30 anos, bonito e bem vestido, atravessou a cidade tocando uma flauta de prata, e 130 crianças o seguiram para fora dos portões e desapareceram sem deixar rastro. Segundo discussões dos registros da cidade, uma anotação de 1384 dizia: "Faz 100 anos que nossas crianças partiram". Há séculos de pesquisa e nenhuma explicação aceita por todos. Entre as hipóteses estão um afogamento no rio Weser, um deslizamento de terra, uma epidemia e a emigração. O site oficial de Hamelin apresenta como a mais plausível a de que os "filhos de Hamelin" eram jovens recrutados para colonizar terras no leste da Europa; sobrenomes comuns em Hamelin na época aparecem com frequência surpreendente em regiões perto de Berlim. Os ratos, que viraram o centro da história, não aparecem nos relatos anteriores a cerca de 1559.

fontes.trecho: The earliest mention of the story seems to have been on a stained-glass window placed in the Church of Hamelin c. 1300. The window was described in several accounts between the 14th and 17th centuries. It was destroyed in 1660. [...] It features the colourful figure of the Pied Piper and several figures of children dressed in white. The window is generally considered to have been created in memory of a tragic historical event for the town. According to multiple secondary discussions of Hamelin’s town records, an entry dated 1384 stated: "It is 100 years since our children left." Although research has been conducted for centuries, no explanation for the historical event is universally accepted as true. In any case, the rats were first added to the story in a version from c. 1559 and are absent from earlier accounts. [...] The Lüneburg manuscript (c. 1440–50) gives an early German account of the event. [...] Heinrich Spanuth, discovered the earliest version of the story in the Lüneburg city archives in 1936. [...] in this Year of Our Lord, 1284, on the Feast of Saints John and Paul. A certain young man thirty years of age, handsome and well-dressed, so that all who saw him admired him because of his appearance, crossed the bridges and entered the town by the West Gate. He then began to play all through the town a silver pipe of the most magnificent sort. All the children who heard his pipe, in the number of 130, followed him to the East Gate and out of the town to the so-called execution place or Calvary. There they proceeded to vanish, so that no trace of them could be found. [...] the children drowned in the river Weser, were killed in a landslide or contracted some disease during an epidemic. [...] Among the various interpretations, reference to the colonization of East Europe starting from Low Germany is the most plausible one: The "Children of Hameln" would have been in those days citizens willing to emigrate being recruited by landowners to settle in Moravia, East Prussia, Pomerania or in the Teutonic Land. [...] The theory is provided credence by the fact that family names common to Hamelin at the time "show up with surprising frequency in the areas of Uckermark and Prignitz, near Berlin."

gancho: O nome saci-pererê se referia de início a um pássaro, o saci, cujo canto parece vir de lugar nenhum. Câmara Cascudo via nele um antigo mito de ave, e a perna única pode vir daí: aves muitas vezes pousam num pé só.
explicacao: O nome vem do tupinambá, e "pererê" quer dizer algo como "saltitante". O saci-pererê do mito se referia originalmente a uma ave da família dos cucos, também chamada de matitaperê. Segundo a tradição, esse pássaro alterna notas agudas e graves que enganam sobre a distância de onde está pousado, e seu canto melancólico parece não vir de lugar nenhum, fazendo viajantes se perderem. Na lenda, o próprio Saci vira esse pássaro para agir sem ser visto. O folclorista Luís da Câmara Cascudo defendeu que o Saci era provavelmente um mito de ave. E um pássaro muitas vezes se apoia numa perna só, o que pode levar facilmente à imagem de um menino de uma perna. A lenda atual mistura tradições tupis com mitos afro-brasileiros e europeus. E boa parte do que se conta hoje sobre o Saci remonta a uma enquete: em 1917, Monteiro Lobato, colaborador de jornal, pediu aos leitores de São Paulo e arredores que mandassem o que sabiam sobre ele, e publicou o resultado em livro em 1918. Detalhes como o cachimbo de barro e o redemoinho em que ele dança faziam parte desse material. Em 1921, Lobato lançou ainda uma versão para crianças.

fontes.trecho: The Saci legend is seen as a combination of native Tupi lore with African-Brazilian and European myth or superstition combined into it. Also, much of the currently told folklore about the Saci is traceable to what writer Monteiro Lobato collected and published in 1917–1918, and the children's book version he created and published in 1921. [...] The term saci derives from Tupinambá: çaci meaning "sick eye", or rather Tupinambá: çua ci "evil eye". The suffixed -pererê also derives from Tupinambá perérég meaning "bouncy, jumpy". The Saci-pererê of myth originally referred to a Cuculiformes (cuckoo family) bird, more specifically the striped cuckoo. [...] Certain details as the smoking the clay pipe, and the ability to create whirlwind and to dance and twirl inside it, were part of the folklore solicited in 1917 from the readership of São Paulo and its periphery by newspaper contributor Monteiro Lobato, subsequently published in book form in 1918. [...] Also in order to do his deeds unseen, the Saci can transform himself into a bird, the striped cuckoo (called Matitaperê, Matita Pereira, or  saci in Brazilian Portuguese), whose melancholic song seems to come from nowhere: that is to say, the bird uses high-pitched and low-pitched calls to falsely simulate the closeness/lowness or distance/height of its perch, thus confusing travelers and making them lose the way. [...] Just as saci is also the name of a bird, the "striped cuckoo", Saci was probably originally an avian myth, as Luís da Câmara Cascudo (1976) has argued. A bird will often perch on just one standing leg, and this can easily lead to the legend that the Saci in human form was one-legged.

gancho: No estreito de Messina, na Itália, miragens que mostram castelos no ar eram atribuídas à magia de Morgana, a feiticeira das lendas do rei Artur. O fenômeno óptico ainda leva o nome dela: Fata Morgana.
explicacao: Fata Morgana é a tradução italiana de Morgan le Fay, a fada Morgana das lendas arturianas. Essas miragens, frequentes no estreito de Messina, eram descritas como castelos de fadas no ar ou terras falsas criadas pela magia dela. O mecanismo é a curvatura da luz. Em tempo calmo, uma camada de ar bem mais quente pode ficar sobre ar frio e denso e formar um "duto atmosférico", que age como uma lente. Os raios se curvam ao atravessar camadas de temperaturas diferentes e, quando essa curvatura fica mais forte que a da própria Terra, descrevem arcos. O resultado é uma pilha de imagens invertidas e direitas de um objeto distante, como um barco, uma ilha ou um trecho de litoral, com faixas comprimidas e esticadas que mudam depressa e muitas vezes deixam o objeto irreconhecível. Uma inversão de temperatura sozinha não basta: é preciso haver o duto, e o observador tem de estar dentro ou abaixo dele. Nas regiões polares, a Fata Morgana aparece sobre grandes mantos de gelo, e lá ela surge em dias relativamente quentes.

fontes.trecho: A Fata Morgana (Italian: [ˈfaːta morˈɡaːna]) is a complex form of mirage visible in a narrow band right above the horizon. The term Fata Morgana is the Italian translation of Morgan le Fay of Arthurian legend. These mirages are often seen in the Italian Strait of Messina, and were described as fairy castles in the air or false land conjured by her magic. Fata Morgana mirages significantly distort the object or objects on which they are based, often such that the object is completely unrecognizable. A Fata Morgana may be seen at sea or on land, in polar regions, or in deserts. It may involve almost any kind of distant object, including boats, islands, and the coastline. Often, a Fata Morgana changes rapidly. The mirage comprises several inverted (upside down) and upright images stacked on top of one another. Fata Morgana mirages also show alternating compressed and stretched zones. The optical phenomenon occurs because rays of light bend when they pass through air layers of different temperatures in a steep thermal inversion where an atmospheric duct has formed. In calm weather, a layer of significantly warmer air may rest over colder dense air, forming an atmospheric duct that acts like a refracting lens, producing a series of both inverted and erect images. A Fata Morgana requires a duct to be present; thermal inversion alone is not enough to produce this kind of mirage. [...] A Fata Morgana is commonly seen in polar regions, where it may be known as an iceblink, especially over large sheets of ice that have a uniform low temperature. [...] In polar regions the Fata Morgana phenomenon is observed on relatively hot days. [...] To generate the Fata Morgana phenomenon, the thermal inversion has to be strong enough that the curvature of the light rays within the inversion layer is stronger than the curvature of the Earth. Under these conditions, the rays bend and create arcs. An observer needs to be within or below an atmospheric duct in order to be able to see a Fata Morgana.

gancho: A foto mais antiga tirada com câmera que sobreviveu, feita por Niépce em 1827, costuma ser descrita como fruto de oito horas de exposição. O museu que a guarda fala em vários dias. E ela ficou sumida por 47 anos.
explicacao: Nicéphore Niépce fez a imagem entre junho e julho de 1827, na sua propriedade de Le Gras, no interior da França: são telhados e o campo vistos de uma janela alta. Sobrevivem mais de vinte heliografias dele, feitas entre 1825 e 1829, mas esta é a única vista feita com câmera que se conhece; as demais que ele mostrou na Inglaterra eram cópias de obras de arte feitas por contato. Ele usou uma câmara escura para projetar a cena sobre uma placa de estanho com chumbo, coberta por uma camada fina de betume da Judeia, um asfalto natural. Onde batia mais luz, o betume endurecia; nas partes escuras, continuava solúvel e era removido com uma mistura que levava óleo de lavanda. A conta tradicional de oito horas vem de um detalhe da imagem: o sol ilumina os prédios dos dois lados, como se tivesse passado de um lado para o outro. Mas um pesquisador moderno que estudou as anotações de Niépce e refez o processo concluiu que a exposição deve ter durado vários dias, e o Harry Ransom Center, da Universidade do Texas, onde a placa está, também descreve vários dias ao sol. Depois de uma última exibição pública em 1905, a imagem caiu no esquecimento por 47 anos, até que os historiadores Helmut e Alison Gernsheim a localizaram em 1952. Hoje ela fica numa vitrine sem oxigênio, monitorada o tempo todo.

fontes.titulo: View from the Window at Le Gras
fontes.trecho: is the oldest surviving photograph. It was created by French inventor Nicéphore Niépce between June 4 and July 18, 1827, in Saint-Loup-de-Varennes, France, and shows parts of the buildings and surrounding countryside of his estate, Le Gras, as seen from a high window. [...] Niépce captured the scene with a camera obscura projected onto a [...] pewter plate thinly coated with bitumen of Judea, a naturally occurring asphalt. The bitumen hardened in the brightly lit areas, but in the dimly lit areas it remained soluble and could be washed away with a mixture of lavender oil and white petroleum. [...] Sunlight strikes the buildings on opposite sides, suggesting an exposure that lasted about eight hours, which has become the traditional estimate; however, a modern researcher who studied Niépce's notes and recreated his processes found that the exposure must have continued for several days. [...] View from the Window at Le Gras was last publicly shown in 1905 and then fell into obscurity for 47 years. [...] Historians Helmut Gernsheim and his wife, Alison Gernsheim, tracked down the photograph in 1952 [...] the metal plate is pewter (tin alloyed with lead [...] in a continuously monitored, stabilized, oxygen-free environment. [...] View from the Window at Le Gras was the only example of a camera photograph; the rest were contact-exposed copies of artwork.

fontes.titulo: The Niépce Heliograph (Harry Ransom Center, Universidade do Texas)
fontes.trecho: He inserted the plate into a camera obscura and positioned it near a window in his second-story workroom. After several days of exposure to sunlight, the plate yielded an impression of the courtyard, outbuildings, and trees outside. [...] More than twenty of Niépce's heliographic plates and prints made between 1825 and 1829 are held in public and private collections, yet the Niépce Heliograph is the only known surviving point de vue.

gancho: A foto tida como a mais antiga com gente, de cerca de 1838, mostra uma avenida movimentada de Paris que parece vazia: só um homem que mandava engraxar as botas (e o engraxate) ficou parado o bastante para aparecer.
explicacao: Louis Daguerre fez a imagem do Boulevard du Temple da janela do seu estúdio, às oito da manhã, num dia entre 24 de abril e 4 de maio de 1837 ou 1838. A rua devia estar cheia de gente e de cavalos, mas a exposição levava de quatro a cinco minutos, e tudo o que se movia sumiu. Ficaram duas figuras quase imóveis numa esquina: um homem com as botas sendo engraxadas e, ao que tudo indica, o engraxate, embora haja quem especule que a segunda figura seja uma bomba d'água. Quando a placa foi exposta em Munique, uma revista de Leipzig já comentava o homem que devia estar extremamente quieto. É, segundo a visão mais aceita, a foto mais antiga que sobreviveu com um ser humano, mas talvez não a primeira: Hippolyte Bayard disse ter feito autorretratos em 1837, que não sobreviveram. A placa original, já deteriorada, foi ainda mais danificada por uma restauração malsucedida a partir de 1970, e as reproduções de hoje vêm de cópias do historiador Beaumont Newhall. Em 15 de outubro de 2026, uma placa comemorativa foi instalada na Place de la République, no ponto exato em que as duas pessoas estavam.

fontes.trecho: is one of the earliest surviving daguerreotype plates produced by Louis Daguerre. Although the image seems to be of a deserted street, it is widely considered to be the earliest surviving photograph to include an image of a human. [...] The photograph was taken at 8:00 AM between 24 April and 4 May, either in 1837 or 1838, from a window in Daguerre's studio [...] The Boulevard du Temple would have been busy with people and horse traffic, but because an exposure time of four to five minutes would have been required, the only people recorded were two keeping still – a bootblack and his customer, at the corner of the street shown at lower left of the plate. It has been speculated, however, that this is not a bootblack, but a water pump. [...] The triptych was put on display at the Munich Arts Association where it immediately attracted attention, with the Leipzig Pfennig-Magazin saying of the 8:00 AM image that "there appeared to be a man having his boots polished who must have been standing extremely still." [...] in 1936 or 1937, the American historian of photography Beaumont Newhall rediscovered them and made reproductions [...] in 1970, they were given out on loan to the Munich City Museum. Restoration was attempted, but ended in disaster, ruining the originals even further. Since then, daguerreotype facsimiles have been reproduced from Newhall's copies. [...] There may have been photographs of people before 1838. Hippolyte Bayard claimed to have taken photographic self-portraits in 1837, but these have not survived. [...] On 15 October 2026, a memorial plaque to the photograph and the two people coincidentally captured on it was unveiled on Place de la République. [...] is located at precisely the location the two people were at in 1838. [...] The images were stored at the royal palace and later at the Bavarian National Museum archives, where they gradually deteriorated

gancho: Nas fotos antigas ninguém sorria só por causa do longo tempo de exposição? Nos anos 1850 já dava para fotografar em segundos. Pesava mais a etiqueta: sorriso largo lembrava bebedeira, loucura e vulgaridade.
explicacao: A parte técnica é real: nos primeiros retratos em daguerreótipo, a exposição passava de 15 minutos, e apoios de pescoço e de cabeça seguravam o modelo no lugar. Um sorriso mantido por tanto tempo virava careta. Mas o tempo de exposição caiu depressa, e um curador do George Eastman Museum lembra que, já nos anos 1850, era possível, em boas condições, fazer fotos com poucos segundos. Mesmo assim, o sorriso só começou a virar a expressão padrão a partir dos anos 1920. O motivo principal era cultural: a fotografia de estúdio herdou as convenções do retrato pintado, em que mostrar os dentes num sorriso largo era associado à lascívia, à loucura, à bebedeira e às classes baixas. Em Londres, o fotógrafo Richard Beard pedia aos clientes que dissessem "prunes" (ameixas secas), para obter uma boca pequena e contida, vista como sinal de decoro. Os dentes ruins da época também entram na conta, embora haja historiadores que duvidem desse fator. A virada veio com a foto amadora: a partir da câmera Kodak de 1888, a propaganda da empresa ligou a fotografia a momentos de lazer e felicidade, e o sorriso foi aos poucos tomando conta dos retratos.

fontes.trecho: The exposure time for early photographs was long: over 15 minutes in the earliest days of the portrait daguerreotype. Though this rapidly decreased to just over a minute as scientists fine-tuned the process, sitters had to remain still the entire time to avoid blur. Neck braces and head clamps, such as this one, were commonly used to hold sitters in place. A natural smile could easily turn into a grimace when held for so long. [...] Much early studio photography in Europe and North America reflected the conventions of Western European portraiture [...] Smiling widely and showing your teeth wasn't a good look for anyone who wanted to be considered a serious person. As scholars such as Angus Trumble and Nicholas Jeeves have detailed, a broad grin was associated with lewdness, lunacy, drunkenness, and the lower classes. [...] In London, daguerreotypist Richard Beard instructed sitters to "say prunes" before their portrait was made, to achieve the perfect tart mouth—then considered the very image of decorum. [...] With the advent of snapshot photography in 1888, Kodak marketed to the world a vision of photography as a joyous pursuit.

fontes.titulo: Now You Know: Why Do People Always Look So Serious in Old Photos? (TIME)
fontes.trecho: it took until the 1920s and ’30s for smiles to start becoming the standard expression in photographs. [...] Some dismiss the idea that bad teeth could have been a possible cause for early photography’s close-lipped images [...] says Todd Gustavson, technology curator at the George Eastman Museum. [...] But he says that technology has been overplayed as the limiting factor. By the 1850s and ’60s it was possible in the right conditions to take photographs with only a few seconds of exposure time

gancho: Pintores retratavam o cavalo a galope com as patas esticadas para a frente e para trás, todas no ar. Em 1878, as fotos de Muybridge mostraram que as quatro saem do chão, sim, mas encolhidas sob o corpo.
explicacao: Leland Stanford, industrial e ex-governador da Califórnia, criava cavalos de corrida e estava convencido de que as pinturas da época mostravam errado o animal correndo. Em 1873, contratou o fotógrafo Eadweard Muybridge, mas a primeira tentativa rendeu só uma imagem borrada. Em 15 de junho de 1878, numa pista de Palo Alto, Muybridge montou uma bateria de 12 câmeras diante de um fundo branco. No primeiro teste, um cavalo a trote puxava uma charrete: fios sob a pista eram acionados um a um pela roda, interrompiam um circuito elétrico e disparavam os obturadores em sequência, com exposições que, segundo se anunciou, duravam um milésimo de segundo. Logo depois, a égua Sallie Gardner passou pela pista a galope. As fotos revelaram posições tão estranhas que muita gente achou ridículas, mas a quantidade de imagens publicadas e as animações em zootrópios venceram as dúvidas. Elas mostraram que os quatro cascos de fato ficam no ar, mas no momento em que as pernas estão recolhidas sob o corpo. Já a famosa aposta de US$ 25 mil que Stanford teria feito sobre o assunto nunca foi comprovada. Muybridge depois projetou versões pintadas das sequências com o seu zoopraxiscópio: é a mais antiga exibição conhecida de imagens em movimento feitas a partir de registros reais.

fontes.trecho: Muybridge's work was commissioned by Leland Stanford, the industrialist, former Governor of California, and horseman [...] Stanford was convinced that most depictions of running horses made by human artists were wrong. The great majority of oil paintings at the time portrayed the animal above the ground with its forelegs both extended forward at the same time as its rear legs were both extended to the rear [...] In 1873, Stanford approached Muybridge to photograph his favorite trotter Occident in action. [...] Nonetheless, the best result was a very blurry and shadowy image of the trotting horse. [...] Wires ran under the surface, from a battery of 12 cameras [...] On 15 June 1878, in the presence of invited turfmen and members of the press, Stanford's racehorse Abe Edgington was sent trotting [...] with the sulky wheel tripping all the wires one by one, breaking the electrical circuit and thus causing each camera shutter to open in turn, for a duration that was claimed to last the 1/1000 part of a second. [...] The photographs showed that all four feet are sometimes simultaneously off the ground and that when galloping this occurs when the feet are "gathered" beneath the body, not when the fore and hindlimbs are "extended" as sometimes depicted in older paintings. [...] Some of the registered positions were deemed ridiculous and seemed off to many people [...] would be smothered by the evidence in the large number of pictures that were published, by the praise of experts, by looking at animations of the sequences in zoetropes [...] The projection of moving painted versions of Muybridge's pictures with the zoopraxiscope was the earliest known motion picture exhibition based on actual recordings of motion. [...] After the first successful experiment, running mare Sallie Gardner was sent across the track.
There are stories that Stanford had made a $25,000 bet on his theories about horse locomotion, but no evidence has been found of such a wager.

gancho: A plateia que fugiu apavorada do trem dos irmãos Lumière provavelmente nunca existiu: não há relato da época de pânico. A história pode ter nascido de comédias que zombavam de caipiras no cinema.
explicacao: O curta "A chegada de um trem à estação de La Ciotat", de uns 50 segundos, mostra uma locomotiva a vapor entrando numa estação do sul da França. Ao contrário do que se costuma dizer, ele nem fez parte da primeira sessão pública dos Lumière, em 28 de dezembro de 1895, em Paris: só foi exibido em janeiro de 1896, em Lyon. O historiador Martin Loiperdinger observa que não existem relatos da época sobre espectadores em pânico, o que, nas salas lotadas de então, provavelmente teria causado feridos e aparecido nos jornais locais. Houve, sim, quem se assustasse: o escritor Máximo Gorki descreveu a impressão de que a máquina ia mergulhar na escuridão da plateia. O pesquisador Stephen Bottomore juntou muitos relatos de sustos, mas nenhum caso confirmado de alguém que acreditasse que o trem era real. Já em 1901 havia comédias mostrando um homem do campo que foge da tela ao ver um trem chegando, e Loiperdinger sugere que essa piada às custas dos caipiras pode ter alimentado a crença. Outra hipótese é a confusão com uma versão em 3D que Louis Lumière refilmou e exibiu em 1934.

fontes.titulo: L'Arrivée d'un train en gare de La Ciotat
fontes.trecho: Contrary to popular belief, it was not shown at the Lumières' first public film screening on 28 December 1895 in Paris, France: the programme of ten films shown that day makes no mention of it. Its first public showing took place in January 1896 in Lyon. [...] This 50-second silent film shows the entry of a train pulled by a steam locomotive into the Gare de La Ciotat, the train station of the French southern coastal town of La Ciotat [...] Martin Loiperdinger notes that there are no contemporary reports of audiences panicking at the sight, which likely would have caused injuries in the crowded exhibition rooms of the era and probably would have received coverage in local newspapers. [...] Russian journalist Maxim Gorky wrote: "A train appears on the screen. It speeds right at you—watch out! It seems as though it will plunge into the darkness in which you sit [...] Bottomore collected many other anecdotes about audience reactions to L'Arrivée d'un Train and similar films, finding many firsthand accounts of spectators being startled or frightened by the images on the screen, but no confirmed instances of people actually believing that it was real. As early as 1901, filmmakers parodied the idea of past audiences being terrified by L'Arrivée d'un Train, making comedic motion pictures that showed a naive rural person attending a showing and then fleeing in terror at the sight of an approaching train on the screen [...] Loiperdinger suggests that this joke at the expense of "country rubes" may have provided the basis for the widespread belief that audiences really reacted that way. [...] Louis Lumière eventually re-shot L'Arrivée d'un Train with a stereoscopic film camera and exhibited it (along with a series of other 3D shorts) at a 1934 meeting of the French Academy of Science. Given the contradictory accounts that plague early cinema and pre-cinema accounts, it is plausible that early cinema historians conflated the audience reactions at these separate screenings

gancho: Em 1888, Louis Le Prince filmou a família num jardim na Inglaterra: é tido como o filme mais antigo que sobreviveu. Dois anos depois, ia pegar um trem para Paris e sumiu. Nem a bagagem foi achada.
explicacao: Le Prince, inventor francês radicado em Leeds, usou uma câmera de lente única e filme de papel da Eastman. Em 14 de outubro de 1888, filmou o filho Adolphe, os sogros e uma amiga caminhando no jardim da casa dos sogros; a sogra morreu dez dias depois. O trabalho dele parece anteceder o de outros pioneiros, como os irmãos Lumière e a equipe de Thomas Edison. Em setembro de 1890, ele se preparava para viajar aos Estados Unidos, supostamente para apresentar o invento, e antes foi a Dijon visitar o irmão. Em 16 de setembro, partiu para Paris de trem, mas os amigos que o esperavam descobriram que ele não estava a bordo. A polícia francesa, a Scotland Yard e a família procuraram sem sucesso, e as teorias vão de assassinato a suicídio, sem prova conclusiva. A viúva suspeitou de crime ligado à disputa de patentes com Edison, mas nunca surgiu prova concreta disso. Em 1898, o filho Adolphe depôs contra Edison num processo em que o americano se dizia o único inventor do cinema, na esperança de ver o pai reconhecido; o caso foi perdido. Três anos depois, Adolphe se matou com um tiro. Em 2003, surgiu nos arquivos da polícia de Paris a foto de um afogado de 1890 muito parecido com Le Prince, mas há quem diga que o corpo era baixo demais para ser o dele.

fontes.trecho: In October 1888, Le Prince filmed moving-picture sequences of family members in Leeds, in the 1888 short films Roundhay Garden Scene, and Accordion Player (showing his son Adolphe Le Prince playing the accordion), using his single-lens camera and Eastman's paper negative film. [...] His work appears to precede the inventions of his contemporaries, such as Friese-Greene and Donisthorpe as well as being years ahead of the Lumière brothers and Dickson (who did the moving image work for Thomas Edison). Le Prince disappeared on 16 September 1890. Numerous conspiracy theories emerged about his disappearance, including murder, disappearance in order to start a new life, and suicide. However, no conclusive evidence was found for any of these theories. [...] In September 1890, Le Prince was preparing for a trip to the United States, supposedly to publicly premiere his work and join his wife and children. Before this journey, he decided to return to France to visit his brother in Dijon. Then, on 16 September, he took a train to Paris, but having taken a later train than planned, his friends in Paris discovered that he was not on board. He was never seen again by his family or friends, nor was the luggage he was traveling with ever found. [...] The French police, Scotland Yard and the family undertook exhaustive searches, but never found him. [...] His widow assumed foul play though no concrete evidence has ever emerged [...] In 1898, Le Prince's elder son Adolphe, who had assisted his father in many of his experiments, was called as a witness for the American Mutoscope Company in their litigation with Edison [...] Three years later, 28-year-old Adolphe was found dead on Fire Island near New York, having died by suicide by shooting himself through his forehead. [...] A photograph of a drowned man pulled from the Seine in 1890, strongly resembling Le Prince, was discovered in 2003 during research in the Paris police archives. [...] However, it has been claimed that the body was too short to be Le Prince. [...] in which Edison claimed to be the first and sole inventor of cinematography [...] Le Prince's widow Lizzie and Adolphe hoped that this would gain recognition for Le Prince's achievement, but when the case went against Mutoscope their hopes were dashed.

is a short silent motion picture filmed by French inventor Louis Le Prince at Oakwood Grange in Roundhay, Leeds, in Yorkshire, England on 14 October 1888. It is believed to be the oldest surviving film. [...] Oakwood Grange, the home of Joseph and Sarah Whitley [...] Joseph (1816–1891) and Sarah (née Robinson, 1816–1888) were the parents of Elizabeth, Louis Le Prince's wife, and Hartley is believed to have been a friend of the Le Princes. Sarah Whitley died ten days after the scene was filmed.

gancho: Em 1929, centenas de rolos de filmes mudos serviram de aterro para nivelar um rinque de hóquei no Yukon, no Canadá. O solo congelado os conservou, e em 1978 uma obra os trouxe de volta.
explicacao: Dawson City, cidade da corrida do ouro do Klondike, exibia filmes desde 1903. Os rolos que não eram devolvidos ficavam guardados num banco local e depois no porão da biblioteca da cidade. A associação esportiva tinha transformado uma piscina num rinque de gelo, mas a conversão malfeita deixava o gelo com temperatura irregular no meio. Em 1929, Clifford Thomson, funcionário do banco e tesoureiro da associação de hóquei, resolveu os dois problemas de uma vez: empilhou na piscina 500 mil pés de filme (cerca de 150 km de película), cobriu tudo com tábuas e nivelou com uma camada de terra. Os filmes de nitrato que continuaram chegando depois ajudaram a alimentar o incêndio que destruiu o complexo em 1951. Os enterrados, protegidos pelo permafrost, sobreviveram. Em 1978, a escavação para um novo centro de recreação revelou 533 rolos com 372 títulos, feitos entre 1903 e 1929, incluindo filmes dados como perdidos e imagens raras da World Series de beisebol de 1919. Para algumas produtoras, essas cópias são o último registro que restou. Por serem quimicamente instáveis, os rolos foram levados em transporte militar para os arquivos nacionais do Canadá e para a Biblioteca do Congresso dos EUA.

fontes.trecho: The Dawson Film Find (DFF) was the accidental discovery in 1978 of 372 film titles preserved in 533 reels of silent-era nitrate films in the Klondike Gold Rush town of Dawson City, Yukon, Canada. The reels had been buried under an abandoned hockey rink in 1929 and included lost films of feature movies and newsreels. [...] The 533 film reels date "between 1903 and 1929 [...] rare footage of historic events, including the 1919 World Series. [...] Beginning in 1903, the Dawson Amateur Athletic Association (DAAA) began showing films in Dawson City, Yukon, Canada. The unreturned films were deposited in the local Canadian Bank of Commerce and later stored in the local Carnegie Library basement. The DAAA later converted a swimming pool to an ice rink, but because of improper conversion the ice rink suffered from uneven temperatures in the middle of the rink. In 1929, Clifford Thomson, then employed by the Canadian Bank of Commerce and also treasurer of the hockey association, solved the problem of the library's stock of film and the inadequate ice rink. Thomson took 500,000 feet of film and stacked the reels in the pool, covered the reels with boards and leveled the rink with a layer of earth. The DAAA continued to receive new nitrate films which would later fuel the destruction of the entire complex in a fire in 1951. The films stored under the ice rink were preserved by permafrost and were later uncovered in 1978 when a new recreation center was being built. The Dawson Film Find material was collected and preserved, with these prints becoming the last surviving records of some movie studios. Owing to its dangerous chemical volatility, the historical find was moved by military transport to Library and Archives Canada and the U.S. Library of Congress

gancho: O filme de nitrato do cinema antigo queima até debaixo d'água: ele traz o próprio oxigênio. Em 1937, numa onda de calor, um depósito pegou fogo sozinho e destruiu a maior parte dos filmes mudos da Fox.
explicacao: Por décadas, a película de cinema foi feita de nitrocelulose, o chamado filme de nitrato. Ao contrário da maioria dos materiais inflamáveis, ela não precisa de ar para continuar queimando, porque a própria molécula contém oxigênio suficiente para manter a chama. Um filme de treinamento para projecionistas mostrava um rolo aceso que seguia queimando mesmo totalmente submerso, e mergulhar o filme em chamas na água pode não apagá-lo e ainda aumentar a fumaça. Com o tempo, o nitrato se decompõe num processo que se acelera sozinho e solta gases. Em julho de 1937, em Little Ferry, Nova Jersey, uma onda de calor com máximas de 38 °C, somada aos gases do filme em decomposição e à ventilação ruim, causou combustão espontânea num depósito da 20th Century-Fox. Mais de 40 mil rolos de negativos e cópias viraram cinza dentro das latas, e um menino de 13 anos que morava perto morreu queimado. Mais de 75% dos longas da Fox anteriores a 1930 estão completamente perdidos. Incêndios, decomposição e o descarte deliberado de filmes velhos explicam por que a grande maioria dos filmes mudos se perdeu. No Reino Unido, até hoje é proibido mandar filme de nitrato pelo correio.

fontes.trecho: A training film for projectionists included footage of a controlled ignition of a reel of nitrate film, which continued to burn even when fully submerged in water. Once burning, it is extremely difficult to extinguish. Unlike most other flammable materials, nitrocellulose does not need a source of air to continue burning, since it contains sufficient oxygen within its molecular structure to sustain a flame. For this reason, immersing burning film in water may not extinguish it, and could actually increase the amount of smoke produced. Owing to public safety precautions, the United Kingdom's Health and Safety Executive to this day forbids transportation of nitrate film by post or public transit [...] Many films produced during the early 20th century were lost through this accelerating, self-catalyzed disintegration or through studio warehouse fires, and many others were deliberately destroyed specifically to avoid the fire risk.

The early motion-picture industry primarily used film stock made of nitrocellulose, commonly called nitrate film. [...] In Little Ferry, gasses produced by decaying film, combined with high temperatures and inadequate ventilation, resulted in spontaneous combustion. [...] Northern New Jersey experienced a heat wave in July 1937, with daytime temperatures of 100 °F (38 °C) and warm nights. [...] All three were seriously burned, and 13-year-old Charles died from his injuries on July 19. [...] with more than 40,000 reels of negatives and prints burned to ashes inside their film cans. [...] more than 75% of Fox's feature films from before 1930 are completely lost.
The vast majority of the silent films produced in the late 19th and early 20th centuries are considered lost.

gancho: Por décadas, laboratórios calibraram as cores das fotos pelo retrato de uma mulher branca, a "Shirley", nome da primeira modelo, funcionária da Kodak. O filme favorecia a pele clara; Godard chegou a recusá-lo.
explicacao: Os cartões Shirley surgiram em meados dos anos 1950. Em 1954, o governo americano agiu para quebrar o monopólio da Kodak, que então vendia quase todo o filme colorido do país e também o revelava em suas lojas. A empresa criou uma impressora para laboratórios independentes e mandava junto um kit com fotos de referência, para que cada laboratório conferisse se as cores e a densidade batiam. A modelo das fotos era Shirley Page, funcionária da Kodak, e o nome pegou: qualquer modelo que viesse depois continuava sendo "a Shirley". No começo, todas eram brancas, muitas vezes com a palavra "normal" no cartão. Para a pesquisadora Lorna Roth, da Universidade Concordia, no Canadá, a faixa de tons que os filmes registravam, tanto de foto quanto de cinema, era enviesada a favor da pele branca. Havia queixas de que, numa mesma foto com pessoas negras e brancas, parte da imagem saía clara ou escura demais. Em 1978, o cineasta Jean-Luc Godard se recusou a usar filme Kodak em Moçambique, declarando que ele era racista. Nos anos 1970, um fotógrafo da Kodak passou a usar muitos modelos negros nos testes, e a empresa acabou fazendo cartões multirraciais, como um de 1995 com três mulheres de tons de pele diferentes.

fontes.titulo: How Kodak's Shirley Cards Set Photography's Skin-Tone Standard (NPR)
fontes.trecho: Shirley cards go back to the mid-1950s. At the time, Kodak sold almost all the color film used in the U.S. After a customer shot the film, they'd bring the roll to a Kodak store to be printed. In 1954, the federal government stepped in to break up Kodak's monopoly. [...] Kodak came up with its S5 printer for independent photo labs. And to make sure the colors and densities of the prints were calibrated correctly, Kodak sent out a kit with color prints and original, unexposed negatives. [...] Each reference card was an original shot of Shirley Page, who worked as a studio model for Kodak's new products. [...] It was just known as the Shirley. And it didn't make any difference which model came in later to do it. It was still called the Shirley. [...] In the early days, all of them were white and often tagged with the word normal. [...] Lorna Roth is a media professor at Concordia University in Canada who has researched the history of Kodak's Shirley cards. [...] Roth says the dynamic range of the film, both still photo stock and motion picture, was biased towards white skin. In 1978, the filmmaker Jean-Luc Godard famously refused to use Kodak film to shoot in Mozambique because he declared the film was racist. People also complain that photos of blacks and whites in the same shot would turn out partially under- or overexposed. [...] In the 1970s, photographer Jim Lyon joined Kodak's first photo tech division and research laboratories. He says the company recognized there was a problem with the all-white Shirley cards. [...] I started incorporating black models pretty heavily in our testing [...] And Kodak started making multiracial norm-reference cards
In 1995, Kodak designed a multiracial norm reference card. This card showed three women (Caucasian, Asian, African) with different skin colors and brightly contrasted clothing.

gancho: Méliès contou que descobriu o truque de fazer coisas sumirem quando a câmera emperrou: na projeção, um ônibus virou carro funerário. Mas um filme da companhia de Edison já usava o truque antes.
explicacao: Georges Méliès, mágico de palco que virou cineasta, contou a história num texto de 1907. O aparelho rudimentar que ele usava no início vivia rasgando ou travando o filme. Um dia, enquanto filmava a Place de l'Opéra, em Paris, precisou parar por um minuto para soltar a película. Nesse intervalo, pedestres, ônibus e carros mudaram de lugar. Quando projetou o filme, emendado no ponto da falha, viu um ônibus da linha Madeleine-Bastille se transformar num carro funerário, e homens virarem mulheres. Estava criado o truque de substituição: parar a filmagem, mudar algo na cena e retomar com o mesmo enquadramento. Dois dias depois, segundo ele, já fazia as primeiras metamorfoses e sumiços de propósito. O historiador Jacques Deslandes considera mais provável que Méliès tenha aprendido o efeito examinando uma cópia de "A execução de Maria Stuart", filme de 1895 da companhia de Edison em que uma versão primitiva do truque aparece na decapitação. De qualquer forma, foi o efeito mais importante da obra de Méliès. Estudos mostraram que boa parte da ilusão vinha do cuidado dele em casar os quadros na montagem, e a colorização à mão ajudava a disfarçar os cortes.

fontes.trecho: The pioneering French filmmaker Georges Méliès claimed to have accidentally developed the stop trick, as he wrote in Les Vues Cinématographiques in 1907 [...] An obstruction of the apparatus that I used in the beginning (a rudimentary apparatus in which the film would often tear or get stuck and refuse to advance) produced an unexpected effect, one day when I was prosaically filming the Place de L'Opéra; I had to stop for a minute to free the film and to get the machine going again. During this time passersby, omnibuses, cars, had all changed places, of course. When I later projected the film, reattached at the point of the rupture, I suddenly saw the Madeleine-Bastille bus changed into a hearse, and men changed into women. The trick-by-substitution, called the stop trick, had been invented and two days later I performed the first metamorphosis of men into women and the first sudden disappearances [...] According to the film scholar Jacques Deslandes, it is more likely that Méliès discovered the trick by carefully examining a print of the Edison Manufacturing Company's 1895 film The Execution of Mary Stuart, in which a primitive version of the trick appears. In any case, the substitution splice was both the first special effect Méliès perfected, and the most important in his body of work. Film historians such as Richard Abel and Elizabeth Ezra established that much of the effect was the result of Méliès's careful frame matching during the editing process [...] the addition of painted color acts as a sleight of hand technique allowing the cuts to pass by unnoticed.
was a French filmmaker, actor, magician, and toymaker. [...] This same stop trick effect had already been used by Thomas Edison when depicting a decapitation in The Execution of Mary Stuart

gancho: Na Primeira Guerra, o Exército francês confiscou mais de quatrocentas cópias de filmes de Méliès e as derreteu para tirar prata e celuloide, que virou salto de sapato. Arruinado, ele foi vender doces numa estação.
explicacao: Georges Méliès, pioneiro dos efeitos especiais, fez sucesso mundial com "Viagem à Lua", de 1902. Mas viu o filme ser copiado sem controle: segundo um relato, uma cópia vendida para exibição só na Argélia foi parar nas mãos de um funcionário da empresa de Thomas Edison e foi duplicada. Em 1904, Edison e outras companhias americanas vendiam o filme, muitas vezes sem nenhum crédito a Méliès. Anos depois, ao romper o contrato com a produtora Pathé, ficou sem como pagar o que devia a ela; faliu e não fez mais filmes depois de 1912. Na guerra, o Exército transformou seu estúdio principal em hospital e confiscou mais de quatrocentas cópias originais da sua produtora, a Star Films, para derretê-las. Ele próprio chegou a destruir seus negativos. No fim de 1925, quando se casou com a atriz Jehanne d'Alcy, estava esquecido e arruinado, e o casal vivia de uma pequena barraca de doces e brinquedos no saguão da estação Gare Montparnasse. Jornalistas o redescobriram, e em 1931 ele recebeu a Legião de Honra das mãos de Louis Lumière. Dos mais de 500 filmes que fez, só cerca de 200 existem hoje. Uma cópia colorida à mão de "Viagem à Lua", dada como perdida, apareceu em 1993.

fontes.trecho: During the war, the French Army confiscated over four hundred of Star Films' original prints and melted them down to recover silver and celluloid, the latter of which the army used to make shoe heels. [...] Méliès was largely forgotten and financially ruined by December 1925, when he married his long-time mistress, the actress Jehanne d'Alcy. The couple scraped together a living by working at a small candy and toy stand d'Alcy owned in the main hall of the Gare Montparnasse. [...] Eventually Méliès was made a Chevalier de la Légion d'honneur, the medal of which was presented to him in October 1931 by Louis Lumière. [...] Méliès was bankrupt and unable to continue making films. [...] Although he never made another film after 1912 [...] In 1917, the French Army turned the main studio building at his Montreuil property into a hospital for wounded soldiers. [...] only roughly 200 out of over 500 Méliès's films remain in existence today. These factors include Méliès's destruction of his original negatives, the French army's confiscation of his prints [...] When Méliès broke his contract with Pathé in 1913, he had nothing with which to cover his indebtedness to that company.

is a 1902 French science-fiction adventure trick film written, directed and produced by Georges Méliès. [...] reports that Méliès sold a print of the film to the Paris photographer Charles Gerschel for use in an Algiers theatre, under strict stipulation that the print only be shown in Algeria. Gerschel sold the print, and various other Méliès films, to the Edison Manufacturing Company employee Alfred C. Abadie, who sent them directly to Edison's laboratories to be duplicated and sold by Vitagraph. Copies of the print spread to other firms, and by 1904 Siegmund Lubin, the Selig Polyscope Company, and Edison were all redistributing it. [...] Méliès was often uncredited altogether [...] An original hand-coloured print was discovered in 1993

gancho: Há fotos coloridas da Rússia dos czares, de 1909 a 1915: cada cena virava três fotos em preto e branco, com filtros vermelho, verde e azul. Juntá-las com facilidade só foi possível quase um século depois, no computador.
explicacao: Sergei Prokudin-Gorsky, químico que estudou com Mendeleev, percorreu o Império Russo num vagão de trem com laboratório fotográfico, cedido pelo czar Nicolau II, e com licenças para entrar em áreas restritas. O método de três cores fora sugerido por Maxwell em 1855: a mesma cena era registrada em três fotos em preto e branco, cada uma atrás de um filtro. Para ver as cores, era preciso projetar as três imagens sobrepostas, com filtros iguais, num aparelho próprio. Como as três exposições não eram simultâneas, tudo o que se mexia ganhava contornos ou "fantasmas" coloridos. Ao deixar o país, depois da Revolução, cerca de metade do material foi confiscada. Os negativos de vidro restantes acabaram guardados no porão de um prédio em Paris, e a Biblioteca do Congresso dos EUA os comprou dos herdeiros em 1948. Por meio século, só uma centena de imagens foi usada, de tão trabalhoso que era fazer cópias coloridas. Em 2004, um cientista da computação combinou automaticamente as cores dos 1.902 negativos, e as imagens viraram um retrato vívido de um mundo desaparecido às vésperas da Primeira Guerra.

fontes.trecho: Using a railway-car darkroom provided by Emperor Nicholas II, Prokudin-Gorsky travelled the Russian Empire from around 1909 to 1915 using his three-image colour photography to record its many aspects. [...] where Prokudin-Gorsky enrolled in Saint Petersburg State Institute of Technology to study chemistry under Dmitri Mendeleev.
