[...] The method of color photography used by Prokudin-Gorsky was first suggested by James Clerk Maxwell in 1855 and demonstrated in 1861 [...] by capturing it in the form of three black-and-white photographs, one taken through a red filter, one through a green filter, and one through a blue filter. The resulting three photographs could be projected through filters of the same colors and exactly superimposed on a screen [...] When the three color-filtered photographs were not taken at the same time, anything in the scene that did not hold steady during the entire operation would exhibit colored "fringes" around its edges in the resulting color image. If it moved continuously across the scene, three separate strongly-colored "ghost" images could result. [...] Outfitted with a specially equipped railroad-car darkroom provided by Tsar Nicholas II and in possession of two permits that granted him access to restricted areas [...] His photographs offer a vivid portrait of a lost world—the Russian Empire on the eve of World War I [...] Upon leaving the country and exporting all his photographic material, about half of the photos were confiscated by Russian authorities [...] were finally stored in the basement of a Parisian apartment building, and the family was worried about them getting damaged. The United States Library of Congress purchased the material from Prokudin-Gorsky's heirs in 1948 [...] only about a hundred of the images were used in exhibits, books and scholarly articles during the half-century after the Library of Congress acquired them. [...] It was only with the advent of digital image processing that multiple images could be quickly and easily combined into one. [...] In 2004, the Library of Congress contracted with computer scientist Blaise Agüera y Arcas to produce an automated color composite of each of the 1,902 negatives

gancho: Em 1891, Gabriel Lippmann fez fotos coloridas com uma emulsão de preto e branco: um espelho de mercúrio fazia a luz interferir consigo mesma e gravar as cores em camadas finíssimas. Ganhou o Nobel de Física de 1908.
explicacao: No método de Lippmann, uma placa de vidro recebia uma emulsão sensível quase transparente, de grãos finíssimos, com um espelho encostado atrás, originalmente de mercúrio líquido. Na exposição, a luz atravessava a emulsão, batia no espelho e voltava sobre si mesma, formando ondas estacionárias. Isso deixava na emulsão várias camadas escurecidas, separadas por distâncias que correspondem ao comprimento de onda de cada cor. Depois de revelada, a placa devolve a luz branca reforçando só as cores certas, e o resultado reproduz as cores originais usando um processo fotográfico de preto e branco. A imagem só aparece no reflexo de uma luz difusa, num ângulo limitado, e não pode ser copiada com técnicas comuns. O processo exigia exposições demoradas para as emulsões da época, nunca entrou em uso geral e perdeu espaço para as placas autocromo dos irmãos Lumière, mas sobreviveu como experimento de física. A durabilidade dessas placas inspirou uma nova aplicação: guardar dados. Em 2019, 150 amostras gravadas pelo mesmo princípio foram levadas à Estação Espacial Internacional e, após cerca de nove meses de exposição a raios cósmicos, não mostraram sinais de perda de dados.

fontes.trecho: It was invented by French scientist Gabriel Lippmann in 1891 and consists of first focusing an image onto a light-sensitive plate, placing the emulsion in contact with a mirror (originally liquid mercury) during the exposure to introduce interference [...] Lippmann won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1908 "for his method of reproducing colours photographically based on the phenomenon of interference". Images made with this method are created on a Lippmann plate: a clear glass plate (having no anti-halation backing), coated with an almost transparent (very low silver halide content) emulsion of extremely fine grains [...] the light rays which strike the transparent light-sensitive film are reflected back on themselves and, by interference, create standing waves. [...] The result is an image having very similar colours as the original using a black and white photographic process. [...] The colour image can only be viewed in the reflection of a diffuse light source from the plate, making the field of view limited, and therefore not easily copied with conventional techniques. The method was very insensitive with the emulsions of the time and it never came into general use. Another reason Lippmann's process of colour photography did not succeed can be found in the invention of the autochrome plates by the Lumière brothers. [...] Because the photographs are so durable, researchers have reworked Lippmann plates for use in archival data storage to replace hard drives. [...] 150 standing-wave storage samples placed on the ISS during 2019 showed no signs of data degradation after exposure to cosmic rays for nine months.

In the 1890s Gabriel Lippmann discovered a method for color photography based on interference—interaction between light waves. Using a mirror, light was reflected through a photographic emulsion in which the interference phenomenon produces a number of blackened layers. The distance between the layers corresponds to certain wavelengths and can be transmuted into a color image. The method never came into widespread usage, but lived on as a physics experiment.

gancho: O filme mais antigo que se conhece com som gravado ao vivo, de 1894 ou 1895, mostra dois homens dançando ao som de um violino. O som, num cilindro de cera quebrado, só foi ligado ao filme em 1998.
explicacao: O curta foi feito por William Dickson no "Black Maria", o estúdio de Thomas Edison em Nova Jersey, para o Kinetofone, um visor de filmes acompanhado de um fonógrafo de cilindro. Dickson toca violino diante de uma corneta que grava o som num cilindro de cera, enquanto dois homens dançam à frente. Não há sinal de que o filme tenha sido exibido no formato original. Uma cópia muda foi parar no Museu de Arte Moderna de Nova York. O som ficou esquecido: um cilindro numa lata com o nome de Dickson foi achado no laboratório de Edison no início dos anos 1960 e, quando a lata foi aberta, em 1964, ele estava quebrado em dois. Só em 1998 pesquisadores ligaram o cilindro ao filme, mandaram consertá-lo e recuperaram o áudio. O premiado montador Walter Murch sincronizou digitalmente imagem e som, e a versão restaurada foi projetada em 2002. No cilindro, antes de a câmera começar a rodar, um homem pergunta se já está funcionando. Um livro de 1981 afirmou, sem citar fonte, que o filme se chamava "The Gay Brothers"; o título se espalhou, mas não há evidência de que tenha existido.

fontes.trecho: The Dickson Experimental Sound Film is a film made by William Dickson in late 1894 or early 1895. It is the first known film with live-recorded sound and appears to be the first motion picture made for the Kinetophone, the proto-sound-film system developed by Dickson and Thomas Edison. (The Kinetophone, consisting of a Kinetoscope accompanied by a cylinder-playing phonograph [...] The film was produced at the "Black Maria", Edison's New Jersey film studio. There is no evidence that it was ever exhibited in its original format. [...] The film features Dickson playing a violin into a recording horn for an off-camera wax cylinder. [...] In front of Dickson, two men dance to the music. [...] A soundless 35mm nitrate print of the movie, described as precisely forty feet long, was acquired by the Museum of Modern Art [...] The soundtrack was inventoried at the Edison National Historic Site in the early 1960s when a wax cylinder in a metal canister labeled "Dickson—Violin by W.K.L. Dixon with Kineto" was found in the music room of the Edison laboratory. In 1964, researchers opened the canister only to find that the cylinder was broken in two [...] The connection between the film and the cylinder was not made until 1998 when Loughney and Edison NHS sound recordings curator Jerry Fabris arranged for the cylinder to be repaired and its contents recovered [...] award-winning film editor Walter Murch be enlisted on the project [...] By digitally converting the film and editing the media together, Murch synchronized the visual and audio elements. [...] This version was projected on a 20' screen at the Edison National Historic Site on June 1, 2002 [...] On the cylinder, before the camera starts rolling, a man's voice can be heard to say, "I asked if it's working. Is it working already? Go ahead." [...] In his book The Celluloid Closet (1981), film historian Vito Russo discusses the film, claiming, without attribution, that it was titled The Gay Brothers. Russo's unsupported naming of the film has been adopted widely online and in at least three books [...] In addition to there being no evidence for the title Russo gives the film

gancho: Na Inglaterra, em 1917, duas primas de 16 e 9 anos fotografaram "fadas" de papelão copiadas de um livro infantil. Conan Doyle, criador de Sherlock Holmes, publicou as fotos como prova. Só em 1983 admitiram a farsa.
explicacao: Elsie Wright e Frances Griffiths brincavam num riacho no fundo do quintal, na vila de Cottingley, e diziam ir até lá para ver fadas. Para provar, Elsie pegou emprestada a câmera do pai. Ele, fotógrafo amador, logo achou que as figuras eram recortes de papelão, mas a mãe acreditou nelas. As fotos se tornaram públicas em 1919 e chegaram a Arthur Conan Doyle, que as usou para ilustrar um artigo sobre fadas na revista The Strand, no Natal de 1920, tratando-as como prova do sobrenatural. Ao todo, foram cinco fotos. Décadas depois, análises de céticos e de um editor de revista de fotografia concluíram que eram falsas. Em 1983, as primas admitiram: Elsie copiara fadas de um livro ilustrado, recortara as figuras e as prendera com alfinetes de chapéu, jogando tudo no riacho depois. Mesmo assim, as duas sustentavam que tinham visto fadas de verdade. Elsie contou que as duas ficaram envergonhadas de desmentir um homem tão brilhante. Só discordaram sobre a quinta foto, que Frances jurava ser verdadeira; um especialista sugeriu uma dupla exposição acidental, o que explicaria por que as duas diziam, sinceramente, tê-la tirado.

fontes.trecho: They appear in a series of five photographs taken by Elsie Wright and Frances Griffiths, two young cousins who lived in Cottingley, near Bradford in England. In 1917, when the first two photographs were taken, Elsie was 16 years old and Frances was 9. The pictures came to the attention of writer Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, who used them to illustrate an article on fairies he had been commissioned to write for the Christmas 1920 edition of The Strand Magazine. Doyle was enthusiastic about the photographs, and interpreted them as clear and visible evidence of supernatural phenomena. [...] The two girls often played together beside the beck at the bottom of the garden [...] Frances and Elsie said they only went to the beck to see the fairies, and to prove it, Elsie borrowed her father's camera [...] Elsie's father, Arthur, was a keen amateur photographer [...] he dismissed the figures as cardboard cutouts. [...] His wife Polly, however, believed the photographs to be authentic. [...] The photographs became public in mid-1919 [...] Geoffrey Crawley, editor of the British Journal of Photography [...] He also concluded that the pictures were fakes. [...] In 1983, the cousins admitted in an article published in the magazine The Unexplained that the photographs had been faked, although both maintained that they really had seen fairies. Elsie had copied illustrations of three dancing fairies by Claude Shepperson from a book [...] They said they had then cut out the cardboard figures and supported them with hatpins, disposing of their props in the beck once the photograph had been taken. But the cousins disagreed about the fifth and final photograph [...] Elsie maintained it was a fake, just like all the others, but Frances insisted that it was genuine. [...] Both Frances and Elsie claimed to have taken the fifth photograph. [...] suggesting that the photograph was "an unintended double exposure of fairy cutouts in the grass", and thus "both ladies can be quite sincere in believing that they each took it". [...] Elsie said that she and Frances were too embarrassed to admit the truth after fooling Doyle, the author of Sherlock Holmes

gancho: O cinema mudo não era só preto e branco: no início dos anos 1920, 80% dos filmes tinham algum tipo de cor. Foi o som que a fez sumir, porque os corantes atrapalhavam a trilha gravada na própria película.
explicacao: Sem processos práticos de cor natural, as cópias dos filmes mudos eram muitas vezes mergulhadas em corantes, com um código de cores: azul para cenas noturnas, amarelo ou âmbar para o dia, vermelho para fogo e verde para um clima de mistério. Havia também a viragem, que trocava a prata da imagem por sais ou corantes, como o conhecido tom sépia, e a colorização à mão, usada nos EUA desde 1895 e muito explorada pelo francês Georges Méliès. Alguns processos chegavam a cores bastante naturais, com duas cores, como o Kinemacolor e o Technicolor. Quando o som passou a ser gravado na própria película, os corantes passaram a atrapalhar a alta resolução de que a trilha sonora precisava, e essas técnicas foram abandonadas. O Technicolor de três tiras, lançado em meados dos anos 1930, era caro e cheio de limitações. Resultado: por quase quatro décadas, a cor não foi tão comum no cinema quanto tinha sido na era muda.

fontes.trecho: Another misconception is that all silent films lacked color. In fact, color was more prevalent in silent films than in the first few decades of sound films. By the early 1920s, 80 percent of movies could be seen in some sort of color, usually in the form of film tinting or toning or hand coloring, but also with fairly natural two-color processes such as Kinemacolor and Technicolor. Traditional colorization processes ceased with the adoption of sound-on-film technology. Traditional film colorization, which involved the use of dyes in some form, interfered with the high resolution required for built-in recorded sound, and was therefore abandoned. The innovative three-strip technicolor process introduced in the mid-1930s was costly and fraught with limitations, and color would not have the same prevalence in film as it did in the silents for nearly four decades. [...] With the lack of natural color processing available, films of the silent era were frequently dipped in dyestuffs and dyed various shades and hues to signal a mood or represent a time of day. Hand tinting dates back to 1895 in the United States [...] Blue represented night scenes, yellow or amber meant day. Red represented fire and green represented a mysterious atmosphere. Similarly, toning of film (such as the common silent film generalization of sepia-toning) with special solutions replaced the silver particles in the film stock with salts or dyes of various colors. [...] Hand coloring was often used in the early "trick" and fantasy films of Europe, especially those by Georges Méliès.
